title: Luke 7:1–17
context: After teaching about faithful hearing and obedience, Jesus heals a centurion’s servant and raises a widow’s only son at Nain. A Gentile’s remarkable faith and the Lord’s unrequested compassion reveal authority that crosses distance, social boundaries, and death itself.

verses.text: After he had finished speaking in the hearing of the people, he entered into Capernaum.
verses.arminianNotes: The sermon gives way to an encounter in Capernaum. Arminian readers see Jesus’ teaching embodied in mercy toward a household outside Israel’s usual boundaries.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise connect the preceding teaching with Christ’s acts of mercy. His arrival prepares a demonstration of the authority on which disciples may rely.

verses.text: A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and at the point of death.
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion values his dying servant, whose need he cannot remedy by command. Arminian readers see intercession beginning in concern for someone vulnerable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise notice the servant’s value to his master. Neither military power nor social position can secure life; the household needs Christ’s mercy.

verses.text: When he heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant.
verses.arminianNotes: Hearing about Jesus leads the centurion to seek help through Jewish elders. Arminian readers see a response to testimony that turns toward Christ in dependent petition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the importance of hearing and intercession as means of seeking Christ. The elders carry a request for rescue, not an explanation of how grace originates.

verses.text: When they came to Jesus, they begged him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy for you to do this for him,
verses.arminianNotes: The elders appeal to the centurion’s worthiness. Arminian readers distinguish their commendation of his generosity from the humble dependence he will express himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish a favorable reputation from a claim on divine mercy. The elders’ assessment is not Jesus’ declaration that healing can be earned.

verses.text: for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us.”
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion’s love for the nation and synagogue support explain the elders’ affection. Arminian readers see generosity across an ethnic boundary without making benefaction the price of healing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize these concrete acts of kindness. They commend his conduct while reserving the narrative’s emphasis for his faith in Christ’s authority.

verses.text: Jesus went with them. When he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, “Lord, don’t trouble yourself, for I am not worthy for you to come under my roof.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus approaches, but the centurion disclaims worthiness to receive him. Arminian readers see humility that welcomes mercy without insisting on entitlement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the contrast with the elders’ appeal to merit. The centurion depends on the Lord’s willingness and authority rather than his own standing.

verses.text: Therefore I didn’t even think myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed.
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion trusts that Jesus’ word is sufficient even at a distance. Arminian readers see genuine faith receiving a gift it cannot accomplish or deserve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers share this account of dependent faith. Confidence rests in the person who speaks, not in the strength of the centurion’s feelings or a ritual.

verses.text: For I also am a man placed under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go!’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
verses.arminianNotes: His experience of authority helps him recognize the effectiveness of Jesus’ command. Arminian readers see trust expressed through an everyday analogy, not a technique for controlling Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the authority that makes the analogy work. Commands are obeyed within the centurion’s sphere, while Jesus’ greater authority extends even to disease.

verses.text: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turned and said to the multitude who followed him, “I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus commends exceptional faith in a Gentile, challenging assumptions that privilege guarantees trust. Arminian readers see an anticipation of Gentile inclusion through faith rather than ethnic entitlement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grace reaching beyond Israel’s boundaries. The comparison rebukes presumption without rejecting Israel as a people or claiming that all Israelites lack faith.

verses.text: Those who were sent, returning to the house, found that the servant who had been sick was well.
verses.arminianNotes: The messengers find the servant well, confirming Jesus’ word. Arminian readers see mercy answering intercession without physical contact between Jesus and the sick man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the effective result of Christ’s authority. Both traditions locate the healing power in Jesus, not in the centurion’s rank or the messengers’ efforts.

verses.text: Soon afterwards, he went to a city called Nain. Many of his disciples, along with a great multitude, went with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus approaches Nain with disciples and a large crowd. Arminian readers see the scene widening from threatened death to a funeral already underway.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the movement toward a public encounter with death. The coming miracle discloses Christ’s compassion without a recorded request for it.

verses.text: Now when he came near to the gate of the city, behold, one who was dead was carried out, the only born son of his mother, and she was a widow. Many people of the city were with her.
verses.arminianNotes: The dead man is his widowed mother’s only son, making her loss especially grievous. Arminian readers see a particular bereavement, not merely an occasion for displaying power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise attend to the mother’s sorrow. The WEB’s only born describes her one and only son; the account does not require speculation about her future circumstances.

verses.text: When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Don’t cry.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ compassion precedes any recorded petition or confession. Arminian readers see grace taking the initiative, not a reward for making the right request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the Lord’s freely initiated compassion. His comfort will be joined to action; neither tradition should turn this scene into a demand that mourners suppress grief.

verses.text: He came near and touched the coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, arise!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus halts the procession and commands the young man to arise. Arminian readers affirm his life-giving authority without making the miracle settle every question about conversion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see an effective command where human help has ended. The restoration displays power over death, though it is not itself a full account of regeneration.

verses.text: He who was dead sat up and began to speak. Then he gave him to his mother.
verses.arminianNotes: The young man speaks, and Jesus restores him to his mother. Arminian readers see resurrection power serving tender, personal restoration rather than spectacle alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress restored life and the mother’s reunion with her son. The gift answers a grief the crowd could share but could not remove.

verses.text: Fear took hold of all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and, “God has visited his people!”
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd glorifies God and recognizes a prophetic visitation. Arminian readers see a fitting response to mercy, while noting that their words do not exhaust Jesus’ identity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that the miracle reveals God’s saving presence among his people. Reverent fear leads here to praise rather than rejection.

verses.text: This report went out concerning him in the whole of Judea and in all the surrounding region.
verses.arminianNotes: News spreads widely, preparing for John’s disciples to report these events. Arminian readers see testimony carrying the effects of Jesus’ mercy beyond the immediate witnesses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the link between the public miracle and the coming question. Reports spread, but the following passage still calls for discerning Jesus’ identity.
